title: Serving in hard places
tomorrow: what does an acrobat know about helping without burning out?

lines: ART CARDS FOR THE COUNTY JAIL.
cards: Prisons, hospices, shelters: places you can drive past for years without going in.
The leader of Mai's Thursday sit runs a meditation group at the county jail, and she asked if anyone could make simple art cards for the men there. Mai froze.
Then Ava texted that her mom goes to the same jail with her church. In the suttas, the Buddha once walked straight down a road that farmers and travelers begged him not to take.
On that road lived Angulimala, a killer feared across the king's land.

teach.h: HE CAN'T CATCH A WALKING MONK.
teach.b: Angulimala sees a lone monk and runs after him with his sword. But however hard he runs, he can't catch the Buddha, who is only walking. Stop, monk! he shouts.
The Buddha answers: I have stopped, Angulimala. You stop too. I've stopped harming living beings; you haven't.
Something in Angulimala breaks open. He throws his weapons away and asks to become a monk. Later, on his alms round, people throw stones at him, and he bears it.
That's the Buddhist answer to why anyone walks into hard places: the texts insist that even the man everyone fled can stop. Ava's family says something close in their own scripture.
In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says, in the King James words: "I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me."
The shared part is real. Both send people toward the prisoner and the sick, not away from them. The difference is honest too.
In Matthew, what's done for the least of these is done for Christ himself.
In the Angulimala story, the weight falls on the one inside the hard place: he can stop, and wake up, through his own practice. Two reasons, one road toward the jail.

how: Buddhist volunteers and chaplains lead meditation groups in prisons, sit with the dying in hospices, and serve in shelters; the story of Angulimala is often told in that work as a sign that anyone can change.

games.q: what does “serving in hard places” mean?
o: service done only in faraway, dangerous countries
a vow to live inside a prison as a monk for life
walking toward the places others avoid, to help

games.q: the road everyone avoided — tap the pairs.
p: a killer who couldn't catch a walking monk
the stones on the alms round
"I was in prison, and ye came unto me"

s: Angulimala caught up with the Buddha but couldn't harm him
however hard he ran, he couldn't catch the Buddha, who was only walking.
after he became a monk, Angulimala was hit by stones on his alms round
in Matthew, Jesus counts visiting a prisoner as something done for him
"I was in prison, and ye came unto me."

games.q: a classmate says visiting prisons is pointless because people in there never change. using the Angulimala story, what's the reply?
o: the texts insist even the man everyone feared could stop and change
it's worth it anyway, because the visitors earn good karma for themselves
he's mostly right, but visiting is polite, so people should go anyway
games.why: the point of the story is Angulimala himself: he stopped, became a monk, and bore the stones. that's why Buddhists walk toward hard places.

practice: Sit with your hands resting open on your knees, palms up, a posture with nothing to hide and nothing to defend. Bring to mind one hard place near you, a jail, a hospice, a shelter, and the people inside it tonight.
Keep your hands open through the sit.

wordCard.voice: Serving in hard places: walking toward the places others avoid, because the texts say anyone there can stop and change.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: compassion, the wish to ease suffering.

carryVoice: Your line: hard places. Even the man everyone fled could stop. Twenty-four days, and one more road.
